sbh4.2:1.3: Twofold criteria of grossness at every level: (1) the *abiding-quality* (*vihāritā*) of lower planes — both more painful AND less calm-abiding (one criterion with two aspects), and (2) the *lesser life-span* (*alpāyuṣkatarā*) — beings reborn in higher planes live longer cosmologically. The Sanskrit *dvividha* framing at 1.1 and 1.4 confirms the twofold reading; the two qualifiers in 1.2 both modify *vihāritā*, not list two separate criteria. For meditative purposes, the life-span criterion connects felt brevity-of-states at lower planes (states keep dropping away) with felt persistence-of-states at higher planes.
sbh4.2:3.6: *Sac-chidra-sāntara* (with-cleft, with-interval) describes first-jhāna attention as *interrupted* — the *vitarka-vicāra* create momentary clefts where attention falters before re-grasping the object. *Niś-chidra-nirantara* (without-cleft, without-interval) is the second jhāna's seamlessly continuous attention. A precise phenomenological description of the 1st→2nd transition.
sbh4.2:4.6: *Prīti* (rapture) is unambiguously good at first and second jhāna, yet for the practitioner moving to third jhāna it must be recognized as *gross* — as a *citta-kṣobha-kara* (mind-disturbance-maker) that obstructs *nirantarā upekṣā*. The engine of the mundane path: what was the achievement of the prior level becomes the obstruction at the next.
sbh4.2:4.16: *Laghu laghv eva prajñayā pratividhyati* — 'lightly, lightly indeed, by wisdom he penetrates.' The mechanism of third jhāna: *prīti*-traces still arise but are met with quick wisdom rather than effortful suppression. The two stabilizing factors are *smṛti* (mindfulness) and *saṁprajanya* (clear-knowing).
sbh4.2:5.2: The syntax distinguishes what is abandoned from what arises. The rapture-conjoined, mind-agitating factor is abandoned; what arises in the mind is raptureless, calm, fully calmed feeling. Reading the raptureless calm as the mind-agitating factor inverts the third-*dhyāna* transition.
sbh4.2:5.7: The third jhāna is the unique zone where calm-equanimity meets felt happiness. Below it, you get happiness without continuous equanimity; above it, you get equanimity without happiness. Why classical texts sometimes call the third jhāna the most pleasant attainment — it is structurally pleasant in a way no other attainment is.
sbh4.2:6.14: The fourth-*dhyāna* formula is being explained retrospectively. The local quote at 5.7 appears to omit *duḥkha*, but the summation at 5.11 gives the full stock sequence: abandoning pleasure and pain, with prior disappearance of joy and dejection. Asanga explicitly lists breath (*āśvāsa-praśvāsa*) among what is abandoned at the fourth jhāna. The breath itself ceases. A structural marker: if the breath has not become very subtle to the point of apparent cessation, fourth jhāna proper has not been entered.
sbh4.2:6.17: *Aniñjya* — without-movement, unperturbed. *Sarveñjitāyatana* — sphere of all-non-perturbation. The structural feature that makes fourth jhāna the launchpad for the formless attainments and the *abhijñā*. Fourth jhāna is a gateway state, not a destination.
sbh4.2:7.5: The transition from form-realm (4th jhāna) to formless (*ākāśānantyāyatana*) requires releasing three perception-categories simultaneously: form-perceptions (color), obstruction-perceptions (resistance/objects-as-blocks), and manifold-perceptions (the world of things). The release-mechanism: *vairāgya* for the first two, *amanasi-kāra* for the third.
sbh4.2:8.4: The most subtle of the formless transitions. The consciousness that has been resolving on space-as-infinite is *itself* infinite (because its object is infinite). The practitioner shifts the resolve to that consciousness. Formless attainments are recursive applications of the same cognitive operation, not increasingly abstract objects.
sbh4.2:9.3: The mechanism for moving to *ākiñcanyāyatana* is *via negativa*. The practitioner searches for an object beyond consciousness — and *fails to find* one. The failure to find is itself the resolution. 'Nothingness' is not a metaphysical claim about emptiness or void — it is the contemplative recognition that no further object is available.
sbh4.2:10.5: *Naiva-saṁjñā-nāsaṁjñāyatana* — perception is not *ceased* (that would be one of the non-conscious attainments below). The printed perception/non-perception phrase at 9.4 is repetitive and likely corrupt, so the English marks a contextual repair: the state is neither ordinary perception of something, nor the nothingness-perception, nor total non-perception. What remains is *sūkṣmā saṁjñā nimittālambane pravartate* — a subtle perception proceeding with sign-as-object. There is barely-perception. Hence 'neither perception nor non-perception.' This is the structural endpoint of the *laukika* path (*bhavāgra*).
sbh4.2:2.11: Three-epithet synonymy chain on ease of dhyāna-attainment: *nikāma-lābhī* (one who gains at will), *akṛcchra-lābhī* (without trouble), *akisara-lābhī* (without difficulty). The MS reads *akisara-akṛtsna-lābhī* as a single compound, but *a-kṛtsna* ('not-whole') will not parse as 'entirely' and breaks the synonymy. Deleanu (Vol. 1 n. 199), citing BHSD on *kisara* = 'difficulty' and the Pali parallel *akasira-lābhī*, treats *akṛtsna* as a scribal interpolation; Shukla also flagged it as suspect. The English renders the three-epithet sequence; the Sanskrit JSON preserves the MS reading per the emendation policy.
sbh4.2:12.2: Two attainments in which consciousness itself ceases. *Asaṁjñā-samāpatti* is reachable by ordinary persons (*pṛthag-jana*) — serious meditators without supramundane attainment. *Nirodha-samāpatti* requires *ākiñcanya-vairāgya* plus stream-entry-or-higher status — an attainment of the noble path, not just of meditative skill. The latter is the closest mundane experience of *nirvāṇa*.
sbh4.2:13.5: The five higher knowledges: range of supernormal powers, divine ear, knowing minds of others, recollection of past lives, divine eye (passing-and-arising of beings). A sixth, *āsrava-kṣaya* (destruction of outflows), is supramundane and not part of this *laukika*-path treatment. These are far outside the working territory of contemporary lay practice.
sbh4.2:12.5: *saṁjñāśalyaḥ maṁ* — the stray *maṁ* after *śalyaḥ* is a source-level fragment that does not parse cleanly; it is preserved as-is per the emendation policy. The three-fold characterization (*roga / gaṇḍa / śalya* — disease, boil, arrow) is the canonical Buddhist formula for naming saṁjñā as fundamentally unsatisfactory, motivating the unconscious attainment as escape.
sbh4.2:12.9: MS reads *śubhakṛtya*, but no heaven by that name exists in Buddhist cosmology. The intended reading is *śubha-kṛtsna* — the *Śubhakṛtsna* ('Entirely-Beautiful') heaven, the third and highest of the Third Dhyāna realm. The corruption *-tya* for *-tsna* is a standard palaeographic substitution; the parallel passage in Asaṅga's *Abhidharmasamuccaya* (10, 20) confirms. The English restores *[Śubha-]kṛtsna*; the Sanskrit JSON preserves the MS reading per the emendation policy. The pairing with *bṛhatphala* (the highest heaven of the Fourth Dhyāna) marks the joint upper bound of mundane *vairāgya* required for entry into *asaṁjñā-samāpatti*.
sbh4.2:14.1: The 12-saṁjñā framework operationalizes how the five abhijñās are produced. The first five (lightness, softness, space-element, body-mind co-presence, adhimokṣa) prepare the *ṛddhi-viṣaya* (supernatural-powers domain). The next four — past-conduct-recollection, sound-assembly, luminous-form-sign, defilement-induced-form-modification — each yields one further abhijñā (*pūrvenivāsa*, *divya-śrotra*, *divya-cakṣus*/*cyutyupapāda*, *cetaḥ-paryāya-jñāna*). The last three (adhimokṣa redux, abhibhvāyatana, kṛtsnāyatana) yield āryā ṛddhi proper — the noble supernatural power distinguished from illusionist's display by being actually efficacious.
sbh4.2:16.1: Yogācāra *āryā-ṛddhi* / *anāryā-ṛddhi* — the noble-vs-ignoble distinction in supernatural powers. Noble: the resolved transformation actually occurs; the task can be accomplished. Ignoble (e.g., māyākāra, illusionists): only the appearance is produced. The same distinction in different terms grounds the standard Buddhist evaluation of magic vs realization.
sbh4.2:2.1: Restored from PDF 6373-6393. The pre-existing JSON jumped from sbh4.2:1.7 (`yāvat prayoganiṣṭhāphalān manaskārāt tatra viviktaṁ kāmair iti`) directly to current 2.1 (`savitarkasavicāraviviktebhyaścittaṁ vyāvartayitvā...`), dropping the entire glossary unpacking of the first-dhyāna formula (paragraph 2 here) and the *nikāma-akṛcchra-akisara* triple of meditative consummation (apparatus at 2.11). The structure is a classical Yogācāra dhyāna-glossary: each phrase of the formula (*viviktaiḥ kāmaiḥ*, *viviktaṁ pāpakair akuśalair dharmair*, *savitarkaṁ savicāraṁ*, *vivekajaṁ prīti-sukhaṁ*) is defined in turn. The corresponding glossary for higher dhyānas continues from current 2.6 (now 3.6) onward.
sbh4.2:10.9: Restored from PDF 6492-6497. Two canonical Yogācāra similes for the qualitative difference between *dhyāna*-attainment and *ārūpya*-attainment: the dhyāna-attainment is like *descending into the underworld* (a downward, settling motion — the *kāya-samprakhyāna-liṅga*); the ārūpya-attainment is like *falling from space* (a free-fall release from form-perception). These bodily-experience signs are the practitioner's diagnostic for which attainment has been reached.
